highlights.text: treats ب-ض-ع as three separate roots: (1) a portion of a thing — a limb or anything else; (2) a patch of ground; (3) a thing being relieved or satisfied, by speech or otherwise.
Trade goods (bidāʿa) — carried on the same "portion" analogy: a merchant's bidāʿa is a portion of his wealth.
Indefinite number: biḍʿ is what falls between three and ten; it is also said that biḍʿ is seven.
the proverb "like one carrying dates as merchandise to Hajar," said of someone bringing a thing to those who know it better and have more of it
Proverb: tushriṭu l-bidāʿatu — when a man is in need, he spends his stock and whatever he has.
as having four separate root meanings: truthfulness, the imitation of a sound, dry land as opposed to sea, and a plant.
Used indefinitely: "I went out by land (barran) / by sea (baḥran)." Q 30:41: "corruption has appeared on land and sea."
"He treats his kinsman with birr" is, at base, truthfulness in love.
al-Nābigha's line: "I bore Barra (righteousness), and you took on Fajāri (wickedness)."
**fard = the single, solitary one.**
**fard = that which has no counterpart, the unmatched one.**
jāʾū furādā / firādan = they came one after another.
al-Musayyab b. ʿAlas, "in the shade of a solitary lote-tree."
The root's core idea is going down / sinking / an inward depression, branching into geography, the body, raiding, and rest-time.
water sinking into the ground or vanishing into its springs — with the Qurʾānic citation «إن أصبح ماؤكم غَوْرًا», "should your water sink away" (67:30)
الغَار is a cave-like hollow in a mountain (a house-like recess, per al-Liḥyānī; a depression, per Thaʿlab)
المَغَارَة is a synonym, cited from the Qurʾān: «لو يجدون ملجأ أو مغارات أو مدخلا», "if they found a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter" (9:57).
غوّر القوم = they entered the noon-rest, or (in another usage) alighted for it, or traveled during it (with a verse of Imruʾ al-Qays about dogs and a wild bull)
The base meaning is to gather, pluck, or pick fruit from a tree
Noun جَنًى — whatever is gathered/plucked, especially from trees while still fresh.
fruit ready for picking (the word used in Qur'an 55:54)
جَنِيّ (an adjective for fruit "freshly picked," also used for dates cut straight from the tree)
The poet Abū Dhu'ayb uses it figuratively — جَنَى العُلَى, "he gathered/acquired eminence, or nobility."
A ḥadīth is cited: "No wrongdoer shall bring injury save upon himself" (one isn't punished for a relative's crime).
in law specifically a wounding, amputation, or maiming
*kahf* as "like a house hollowed out in a mountain," plural *kuhūf*
the point being that a *kahf* is **wide**, and when small it is called a *ghār*
the verses of Bishr b. Abī Khāzim ("They seek terms of peace at Dhāt Kahf, though there is in it for them neither *salaʿ* nor *qār*")
highlights.note: Bishr b. Abī Khāzim, pre-Islamic; place-name

highlights.text: adhering, sticking fast, not parting.
Ibn Manẓūr notes that since the word also means constancy and persistence, it is treated as though it belonged to the aḍdād (words carrying two contrary senses).
أَلزَمَه إياه (alzamahu, IV): to impose something on someone, so that he then takes it on (fa-iltazamahu).
the entry glosses it as a punishment that cleaves inseparably to the addressees.
the punishment would have cleaved to them
Ṣakhr al-Ghayy: though they escape the death of one land, they have met their deaths lizāman — glossed as: decreed death is inescapable; escape it in one place and it meets you in another.
Abū Dhuʾayb: "he saw nothing but a charging band, lizāman" — here lizām means mulāzim, pressing close
Al-Zajjāj reports Abū ʿUbayda's gloss fayṣalan ("a decisive severance"), and reports that the exegetes as a body took it to mean the Day of Badr and what befell them there
A ḥadīth on the portents of the Hour mentions al-lizām, explained there as the Day of Badr
to nullify, efface completely
maḥaqahu (yamḥaquhu, maḥq) = he abolished it and effaced it until nothing of it remained.
"wa yamḥaqa l-kāfirīn" (Q 3:141), which the author glosses as "He uproots them and nullifies their deeds."
Abū Zayd: "God effaced (maḥaqa) the thing" means He removed its blessing, its good, and its yield.
Illustrated with a verse by Sāʿida ibn Juʾayya al-Hudhalī describing wild asses standing exhausted in the blazing summer heat.
Illustrated with a satirical verse by Sabra ibn ʿAmr al-Asadī
highlights.note: Sabra ibn ʿAmr, pre-Islamic; amḥaqa = perished

highlights.text: to possess or contain a thing and to have the power of sole disposal over it
"He has no malk/milk/mulk" = he owns nothing.
mulk Allāh / malakūt = His dominion and greatness; malakūt of a place = its glory and power.
The possessor of dominion is called malk, malik, malīk, or mālik
By extension, mulūk al-naḥl = the "kings" (leaders) of a bee-swarm (Abū Dhuʾayb cited).
Proverb: "either I perish (hulk) or I gain mastery (mulk)."
to withhold / prevent
is the opposite of "he gave." It is defined as standing between a man and the thing he wants, or "fencing off" a thing.
Zabīdī cites Qurʾānic usage: "they withhold small kindnesses" (māʿūn), "a withholder of good" (mannāʿ li-l-khayr), and "when good touches him, grudging" (manūʿ).
illustrated by a rajaz line ("Withhold them! from the camels…") attributed variously to Bakr b. Wāʾil or Banū Tamīm
the One who withholds from whoever deserves to be denied; or the One who protects the people of His religion
highlights.note: theological reading of the divine name al-Māniʿ

highlights.text: to touch. مَسِسْتُه "I touched it with my hand"
mass is like lams (touching), but mass is used for reaching after / seeking a thing even if it is not attained, while lams implies actual perception by the sense of touch.
The standard Q form لَا مِسَاسَ (Moses to the Samaritan) = "do not touch me" / "no contact," imposed as a punishment of social isolation.
tamāss / mumāssa = mutual touching, and used euphemistically for sexual intercourse: Q "before the two touch each other (yatamāssā).
generally any harm that reaches a person — Q "the Fire will not touch us," "hardship touched them," "harm has touched me," "Satan has touched me."
Shawāhid from Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī.
highlights.note: Dhū al-Iṣbaʿ al-ʿAdwānī, pre-Islamic; for masūs water

highlights.text: to gush/spring forth
This is why a spring is called يَنْبُوع (yanbūʿ, "spring/wellspring") — al-Azharī explains it as a يَفْعُول-pattern noun from the same verb, plural يَنابِيع.
Cited here is the Qur'anic phrase "حتى تَفْجُرَ لنا من الأَرض يَنْبُوعاً" — "until you make a spring gush forth for us from the earth" (cf. Q. 17:90)
a line of Abū Dhuʾayb using يَتَنَبَّعُ for a fate that "wells up"/draws near
To be saved from something: najā (verbal nouns najw, najāʾ, najāt); the forms najjā and istanjā carry the same sense.
Causative "to deliver": najjā and anjā. Qurʾānic: "and thus We deliver the believers" (21:88).
najā / nājā / intajā / tanājā = to speak secretly, whisper, confer privately. al-najwā and al-najī mean both "the secret" and "those conferring in secret."
istanjā al-jāzir watara l-matn = the butcher cut the back-sinew (verse of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān b. Ḥassān).
fewness/scarcity.
Verb قَلَّ يَقِلُّ ("to be few/little"); participle قَلِيل
قَلَّلَ / أَقَلَّ = make little
أَقَلَّ / اسْتَقَلَّ الشيءَ = carry and raise it
"a spreading/flattening out in a place."
a level, low-lying, spacious, firm stretch of ground: no roughness, no rise or dip; the surrounding hills/mountains stand back from it
"then He will leave it a level plain" (Q20:106) and "like a mirage in a lowland" (Q24:39).
"saying, speech." Loosely, qawl is kalām (connected speech).
More precisely (per the exacting grammarian), it is any utterance the tongue produces, complete or incomplete.
qāʾil (speaker), plurals quwwal, qiyyal, qālah (Thaʿlab: "they are qālah — speakers — of the truth")
taqawwala qawlan = to fabricate a saying as a lie.
"he inclined and turned away from something" (māla wa-ḥāda ʿan al-shay').
"Rāgha fulānun ilā fulānin" = he inclined toward someone covertly.
Both are glossed as "a swerving in concealment,"
illustrated by a verse of ʿAdī ibn Zayd al-ʿIbādī ("a day when dodging avails nothing except the resolute, discerning man")
Proverb "arwaghu min thaʿlab," "more evasive than a fox" — quoted from Ṭarafah ibn al-ʿAbd's complaint about disloyal friends
smooth, sweet water: salsal, salsāl, and sulāsil all describe sweet water that goes down the throat easily because of its clarity and sweetness
al-salsala at root means "the joining of one thing to another"
silsila is the familiar linked ring of iron or similar material, derived from that root sense
Cited in verse by Abū Kabīr (salsal wine, i.e. smooth wine, sweeter than the memory of youth), Labīd (sulāsil water among luxury goods in saddle-bags), and Abū Dhuʾayb (water from a mountain-cleft).
highlights.note: Abū Kabīr (pre-Islamic); Labīd, Abū Dhuʾayb (lived into Islam)

highlights.text: A related idea: when such water flows or the wind ripples it, it comes to look like a silsila (chain) — illustrated by Aws's image of wind rippling a pool's surface.
Al-Zajjāj takes it as the proper name of the Paradise spring, meaning something at the height of smoothness.
Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as "it slides down their throats"
A ḥadīth speaks of people "led to Paradise in chains" — explained as captives brought to Islam under compulsion, whose eventual entry into Paradise this describes figuratively, not a literal chain
heaviness, the opposite of lightness.
adjective ثَقيل (heavy), plural ثِقال
A heavy load or burden (ثِقْل, plural أثقال).
أثقل (to load heavily) — cited for Q 52:40 فهم من مغرم مثقلون ("weighed down by debt")
مِثقال — a weight-equivalent, "that whose weight is made known."
Supporting verse of al-Khansāʾ: the earth "adorned itself" with a buried noble man — i.e. adorned its dead through him.
Labīd's verse describes a man who "wakes ثاقلاً," i.e. heavy with illness near death
which Ibn Sīda glosses as the earth's treasures and its dead
Two readings Ibn Sīda records: (a) the heavy religious duty laid upon him; (b) an allusion to the gravity and excellence of the utterance.
خَطْوَةٌ (fatḥa) = one act of stepping, a single step
خُطْوَةٌ (ḍamma) = the span between the two feet, the stride-distance
is explained as "do not follow the ways of the Devil" (per the TA), or "the footsteps of the Devil" (per the JK)
Poetic witness from Imraʾ al-Qays: she bounds like a gazelle, so that "one valley is crossed at a walk and one valley trampled as though rained upon"
